info.bio: The Pointer Sisters, grupo de soul formado en 1971 en East Oakland por las hermanas Bonnie Pointer, June Pointer, Anita Pointer y Ruth Pointer. Desde jóvenes estuvieron influidas por el gospel y el soul de The Staple Singers, Aretha Franklin y The Andrews Sisters. En 1971 firmaron con Blue Thumb Records. Su primer single con cierto éxito fue "Yes we can can", una versión de un tema de Allen Toussaint en 1973. Dos años más tarde llegaron al número uno con el tema "How Long (Betcha' Got a Chick on the Side)".

scenes.name: Divas funky
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Pocas instrumentistas, pero divas que no cedían terreno, casi siempre sin una banda como la de Chaka. James Brown reclutó a Vicki Anderson, Marva Whitney y Lyn Collins; Yvonne Fair hizo The Bitch Is Black en Motown; Millie Jackson construyó tres décadas de descaro; Betty Davis, exmujer de Miles (a quien descubrió a Hendrix y la ropa freak), grabó tres discos de funk ardiente demasiado calientes para Estados Unidos. Clinton fichó a Jessica Cleaves y a las coristas de Sly, Lynn Mabry y Dawn Silva, primeras Brides of Funkenstein («Disco to Go»). Las Pointer Sisters («Yes We Can Can») y LaBelle (Patti LaBelle, Nona Hendryx, Sarah Dash; «Lady Marmalade»), ambas con Allen Toussaint; Tina Turner aguantó a Ike. Demasiadas acabaron al frente de grupos de disco fantasma.
scenes.family: Soul y proto-funk: Stax, Nueva Orleans, Motown

scenes.name: Música disco
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El funk abre la puerta a la subcultura disco: los gays de Nueva York, perseguidos, crean sus islas sociales en clubes privados y recuperan la despersonalización del éxtasis colectivo. Tres hechos la impulsan: el soul orquestal de Barry White, «Autobahn» de Kraftwerk y el Polymoog. Manu Dibango («Soul Makossa») y MFSB la inventan; Giorgio Moroder casa la música robótica de Kraftwerk con el soul (Donna Summer, «I Feel Love», nacimiento del synth-pop). Van McCoy, el maxi de 12" de Walter Gibbons, Chic, Grace Jones, Gloria Gaynor, Saturday Night Fever, el Warehouse de Frankie Knuckles y el Paradise Garage de Larry Levan. Los reyes del pop: Michael Jackson (Thriller, «el mayor farol de todos los tiempos») y Prince, su contrapartida intelectual.
scenes.family: Soul, funk, disco, hip hop y baile

mentions.text: …the "commodization" of disco-music. This was evident, for example, in the gospel-infected singles crafted by producer Richard Perry for the Pointer Sisters, that would become increasingly upbeat, all the way to their 1984 best-sellers (Jump, I'm So Excited and Neutron Dance). The kings of pop 1975-79…

podcast.title: First African American Vocal Group at Grand Ole Opry (1974)
podcast.body: In October 1974, The Pointer Sisters made history by performing "Fairy Tale" at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, becoming the first ever African American vocal group to grace its stage. "culminating in an October 1974 performance of Fairy Tale at the Grand Ole Opera, making the pointer sisters the first ever African American vocal group to perform at the Opera."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Grand Ole Opry Performance (1974)
podcast.body: The Pointer Sisters were invited to perform at the Grand Ole Opry in 1974, four years after Linda Martell's debut, following the success of their hit "Fairy Tale." "Four years after Linda Martell's appearance at the Grand Ole Opry, the pointer sisters were invited to play there."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: New Year's Rockin' Eve Performance (1974)
podcast.body: The Pointer Sisters were among the musical guests who performed on Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve in 1974. "the pointer sisters."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 47 - Dick Clark's Entertainment Empire

podcast.title: Observations of Kinshasa (1974)
podcast.body: Ruth Pointer's observations of Kinshasa, the host city for Zaire 74, described it as a "third world" city with dirt roads and no sidewalks, despite President Mobutu's portrayal of it as modern. She noted the vibrant local life, including women balancing baskets on their heads, street musicians, and unusual local delicacies like "monkey paws stuffed with vegetables." "Mobutu touted Kinshasa as a modern city, but it was as third world as it got."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Spiritual Quest to Zaire (1974)
podcast.body: Ruth Pointer described The Pointer Sisters' trip to Zaire for the festival as a "spiritual quest to connect with our native land and its people," highlighting a broader motivation among African-American performers to explore their heritage. "it was quote, a spiritual quest to connect with our native land and its people."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Grammy Award for Country Performance (1975)
podcast.body: The Pointer Sisters won a Grammy Award for Best Country Performance by a Group or Duo in 1975 for their song "Fairy Tale." They held the distinction of being the only African American women to win a country Grammy for 50 years until Beyoncé's win in 2024. "Fairy tale earned the pointer sisters a Grammy Award... for best country performance by a group or duo in 1975."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Audience Dilution due to Wide Range (1977)
podcast.body: One potential drawback of The Pointer Sisters' diverse vocal projects and genre-crossing was that it arguably diluted their audience, leading to underperforming singles on the charts by 1977. "If there was any downside to the pointer sisters wide range of vocal projects, it's that it arguably diluted their audience."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Transition to Trio (1978)
podcast.body: Following Bonnie Pointer's departure for a solo career in 1978 and a temporary break by June, the group was reduced to a duo of Ruth and Anita, until June was persuaded to return, reconstituting The Pointer Sisters as a trio for their subsequent period of greatest success. "For a brief period, the pointer sisters were reduced to a duo of Ruth and Anita. Youngest sister June took a break from recording entirely."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Andrews Sisters Harmony Inspiration
podcast.body: The intricate harmony arrangements of the Andrews Sisters, particularly on songs like "Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy" and "Don't Sit Under the Apple Tree (With Anyone Else But Me)," significantly inspired The Pointer Sisters, who found they could imitate this pre-rock style. "The intricate harmony arrangements of the Andrews sisters who turned songs like the Boogie Woogie Bugleboy and don't sit under the apple tree with anyone else but me into standards."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Arkansas Country Music Influence
podcast.body: During yearly visits to Prescott, Arkansas, the Pointer Sisters were exposed to country music through a local radio station, with Anita Pointer recalling listening to artists like Hank Williams and Willie Nelson and appreciating the "short story format" of country songs. "There, the pointer sisters were exposed to country music. Anita pointer later recalled, quote, I only remember listening to one Arkansas radio station. And all they played was country music."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Arkansas Roots and Country Upbringing
podcast.body: The Pointer Sisters, hailing from Arkansas, grew up immersed in country music. They listened to it at home, on the radio, and in church, considering themselves "country people." "We were country people. Anita Pointer said."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Band's Refusal to Play Country
podcast.body: The Pointer Sisters' own band refused to record "Fairy Tale," with their drummer stating, "I didn't join this group to play country music." This led the sisters to record the song with Nashville session musicians. "Their drummer got up and left and said I didn't join this group to play country music."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Billboard's Fourth Biggest Girl Group in Chart History
podcast.body: Billboard ranks The Pointer Sisters as the fourth biggest girl group in chart history, following Destiny's Child (third), TLC (second), and The Supremes (first). "Billboard ranks the pointer sisters as the fourth biggest girl group in chart history, after in third place Destiny's Child, in second place TLC, and leading the pack unsurprisingly the Supremes."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Evolution of Group Lineup (Late 60s - 70s)
podcast.body: Bonnie and June were the primary singers in the late 1960s, then second-oldest sister Anita joined to form a trio, and by the 1970s, oldest sister Ruth made them a quartet. "At first, Bonnie and June, the two youngest sisters, were the primary singers. By the late 60s, they were joined by second oldest sister Anita to form a trio. And by the 70s, oldest sister Ruth made them a quartet."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Experience with Racism in Nashville
podcast.body: Upon arriving in Nashville for an event, the Pointer Sisters were mistakenly taken to the back of the venue, with staff assuming they were there to work in the kitchen. They were not there for work but to perform. "The staff thought that they were there to work the kitchen. Nope. They were not. They were there to sing this."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Formative Bay Area Gospel Scene
podcast.body: The Bay Area's gospel music scene was highly influential for the sisters, with June and Bonnie participating in the Northern California youth choir, the same ensemble that produced the Edwin Hawkins Singers' "Oh Happy Day." "by the late 1960s Kernodal writes, The West Coast had become the epicenter of a new wave of music experimentation that would shift the sound and cultural context of black, sacred music during the latter part of the 20th century."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Inspiration for Country Music Entry
podcast.body: Their venture into country music was sparked by heartbreak. Anita Pointer's relationship with a DJ ended when she discovered he was married, inspiring her and sister Bonnie to write "Fairy Tale" in the country genre. "Anita was dating a DJ and he neglected to tell her that he was married. Thus, their love that she thought they had was a fairy tale."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Lambert, Hendricks & Ross Vocalese and Interracial Influence
podcast.body: The Pointer Sisters were particularly inspired by the 1950s vocal trio Lambert, Hendricks & Ross, who pioneered the intricate jazz singing style known as vocalese and were notable for being a co-ed and interracial group. "Who not only helped pioneer the intricate jazz singing style known as vocal ease, they were also coed and interracial joining together the white Dave Lambert and Annie Ross with the black singer John Hendrix."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: No Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Nomination
podcast.body: Despite their indelible hits and broad musical versatility, The Pointer Sisters have never been nominated for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, possibly because their widespread pop chart success prevented their fandom from being "owned" by any single genre audience. "Despite recording some truly indelible hits, the pointer sisters do not enjoy the same status as such rock and roll hall of fame inducted girl groups as Martha and the Vandela's, The Ronets, or The Go-Gos. They have never even been nominated for the rock hall."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Oakland, California Origins
podcast.body: The Pointer Sisters were a family vocal group from Oakland, California, where sisters Ruth (b. 1946), Anita (b. 1948), Bonnie (b. 1950), and June (b. 1953) were born. "a family vocal group from Oakland, California, dropped four straight top ten hits all in 1984."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Strict Religious Upbringing
podcast.body: Raised by Sarah and Elton Pointer in a strict religious household, their father, Elton Pointer, was a pastor at the West Oakland Church of God, and the girls were initially only encouraged to listen to and sing gospel music. "They were all born in Oakland, California, Ruth in 1946, Anita in 48, Bonnie in 1950, and Baby June in 1953, to Sarah and Elton pointer who raised them in a strict religious household."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Unique Multi-Genre Top 40 Success
podcast.body: According to a recent obituary of Anita Pointer, the group holds the distinction of being the only act to have landed top 40 hits on all five of Billboard's country, R&B, pop, dance, and adult contemporary charts, a rare combination for any act, particularly a Black vocal group. "According to a recent obituary of Anita pointer, the pointer sisters are the only group to have landed top 40 hits on all five of Billboard's country, R&B, pop, dance, and adult contemporary charts."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: West Coast Backing Vocal Troupe
podcast.body: Around the early 1970s, the Pointer Sisters became a highly sought-after backing vocal troupe, described as a "west coast version of the Sweet Inspirations," providing vocals for a diverse mix of rock and R&B acts. "It was around this time that the pointers became a well-regarded backing vocal troupe, a kind of west coast version of the sweet inspirations."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1
